items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — never framed what he'd do with the next ten minutes, so the customer set the agenda and drove the whole call
Never confirmed the move date (the 25th) was still available or still held

Almost no probing: no origin/destination addresses, no confirmation of the home size with the customer (he only read 2500 sqft off the record), no stairs or floors, no additional rooms, no boxes, no additional stops, no access or parking concerns, no moving-stressors question
Never covered what's included — gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools — with a customer who was explicitly accusing Einstein of overcharging
No 'no hidden fees' pitch (no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees) — the single strongest available answer to 'you're trying to take advantage of me'
No No Worries Damage Coverage mention, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee — zero differentiators offered to a customer who said he'd call five other movers
No clock explanation — no 'clock starts on-site', no 2.5-hour minimum, no 15-minute prorated increments, which is what makes the hourly model feel fair rather than open-ended
Never stated how many movers or trucks the estimate was built on, and never gave the actual typical hour range for a 2500 sqft home — only referenced that 'typical ranges' exist

Entire Save Your Ass prep speech skipped. This was the highest-value miss on the call: the customer was refusing to pay for packing, and the prep speech is the exact tool for 'here's how you cut hours off the bill yourself'
No attempt to book or hold anything, and no offer to actually schedule the virtual walkthrough he had just argued was necessary — he floated it and let it drop
No confirmation email, no bolded recap, no 'reply with any corrections'
No 'any other questions before I let you go?', no hours, no direct callback number — the customer had to ask his name twice
Volunteered 'I'm actually not one of the managers', 'I can't promise you anything, I can't commit to anything' — undercut his own authority instead of owning the next step
Never used the customer's name once in a 10-minute call, even after Jim introduced himself and asked for Garrison's name twice
Never offered a budget-conscious path forward — no partial packing, no packing-only-the-kitchen option, no way to lower the number
top_strength: He absorbed a genuinely hostile call without getting defensive and diagnosed the real problem correctly — that no virtual walkthrough was ever done, which is why Lucas's verbal number and the emailed quote diverged. He also correctly explained the quote composition (packing runs about as long as the move, so roughly another $3,400) and got a caller who opened with 'we're not gonna pay $7,000' to close with 'Yes, perfect Garrison. That's great.'
coaching_note: When a live deal is on the line, don't end the call with a promise to research — end it with something scheduled. He should have booked the virtual walkthrough on that call, since it was both the fix for the pricing gap and the only thing that keeps Einstein in the running while Jim collects five competing quotes. Second: a price objection is the moment to run the value stack (what's included, no hidden fees, No Worries coverage, On-Time Guarantee) and the prep speech, not to go quiet on all of it.
phone_presence_notes: He stayed calm and steady under real hostility and de-escalated the customer, but the warmth came out as repetitive filler ('absolutely', 'sure', 'I see', 'alrighty') rather than genuine acknowledgment, and he never once used the customer's name.
audio_review_reason: High-emotion escalation with a churn-risk customer — the transcript can't show whether Garrison sounded confident and in control or hesitant and defensive, and his repeated self-limiting statements ('I can't promise you anything', 'I'm not one of the managers') read very differently depending on tone. Worth listening to before coaching him on it.
